## [v1.0.1](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v1.0.1) — 2026-10-28

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v1.0.1

[Diff since v1.0.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v1.0.0...v1.0.1)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v1.0.1

Accuracy of the nonuniform `b` kernels.

##### Highlights

- The ghost values beyond the ends of a nonuniform grid are now computed with the same care as on uniform grids: the extrapolation coefficients are solved in `BigFloat` and the ghost sums are compensated. In `Float64` this removes the boundary floor of the wide kernels on nonuniform grids — `:b13` now reaches machine precision there.
- The nonuniform weight polynomials are stored in the interpolant's element type instead of `Float64`. A `BigFloat` interpolant on a nonuniform grid now converges beyond `Float64` accuracy, at the kernel's full order: 14th for `:b13`, as the [nonuniform benchmark](https://convinterp.org/benchmarks/julia/nonuniform.html) shows.

##### Breaking changes

None.

##### Migration guide

Nothing to do. `Float64` interpolants give the same results as before, except more accurate near the ends of nonuniform grids.

## [v1.0.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v1.0.0) — 2026-10-27

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v1.0.0

[Diff since v0.30.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.30.0...v1.0.0)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v1.0.0

The interface is stable. Everything the package does is documented at [convinterp.org](https://convinterp.org), with benchmarks against the established Julia packages for each capability; the README is now a short front door to that site.

##### Highlights

- One interface for interpolation, derivatives, integrals, smoothing and scattered-data fitting, on uniform and nonuniform grids, in any dimension.
- Kernel weights evaluated exactly from the kernels' polynomial pieces, in any precision, with nothing precomputed or written to disk.
- `fit_scattered` with smoothing chosen by cross-validation, on uniform, adaptive and user-supplied knot grids.
- Only standard-library dependencies: LinearAlgebra and SparseArrays.

##### Breaking changes

- `scattered_to_grid` is removed. Its gridding-and-smoothing pipeline is replaced by `fit_scattered` in its default `:smooth` mode, which is more accurate.
- The keywords `precompute`, `subgrid` and `boundary_fallback`, deprecated and without effect since v0.24 and v0.26, are removed from `convolution_interpolation`, `ConvolutionInterpolation`, `FastConvolutionInterpolation`, `convolution_resample` and `fit_scattered`.
- The NearestNeighbors.jl dependency is dropped.
- Internal struct fields and type parameters left over from earlier evaluation schemes are removed. Code that constructs the interpolation types directly through their inner constructors needs updating; the public constructors are unchanged.

##### Migration guide

- Replace `scattered_to_grid(points, values, knots)` with `fit_scattered(points, values)`, which chooses its own grid and smoothing, or with `fit_scattered(points, values; grid = knots)` to fit on the knots you had.
- Delete any `precompute`, `subgrid` or `boundary_fallback` keyword from your calls; they changed nothing already.
- Nothing else changes: results are identical to v0.30.0 to the last bit.

## [v0.30.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.30.0) — 2026-10-22

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.30.0

[Diff since v0.29.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.29.0...v0.30.0)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.30.0

##### Knots that follow the signal

`fit_scattered(…; mode = :smooth, grid = :adaptive)` now places its knots where the signal
needs them, not where the points are. The uniform fit is made first; the curvature of that
fit along each axis places the knots: dense in a boundary layer, a step or a fast
oscillation, sparse where the fit is flat, and the fit is repeated on them, with half the
uniform fit's knot count by default. On uniformly sampled data, where the point density
says nothing, this reduces both the largest and the rms error, typically by a factor of
two to three, at half the knots. For `mode = :exact` the knots still follow the points,
which is what lets it interpolate clustered data.

##### Boundary rules for smoothing fits

`fit_scattered(…; mode = :smooth)` takes `bc` on uniform grids, in the forms
`convolution_interpolation` accepts: a Symbol, a `(left, right)` pair, or one pair per
axis. `:poly` stays the default; `:linear` or `:quadratic` at an end where the signal is
flat removes the noise amplification of the polynomial ghost rule there. On nonuniform
grids the ghosts are the kernel's own, and `bc` now says so: the default `bc = nothing`
resolves to `:detect` on uniform grids and to `:kernel` on nonuniform ones, and giving any
other rule on a nonuniform grid is an error rather than silently ignored.

##### One default kernel

The scattered-data fits default to `:b5` in one to three dimensions for both modes and
both grid types (`:n3`, `:a4` or `:a3` above that, as before), replacing `:a4` for uniform
`:smooth` and `:n3` for nonuniform `:smooth`.

##### Breaking changes

- `fit_scattered(…; mode = :smooth, grid = :adaptive)` returns different knots than v0.29:
  signal-placed rather than point-placed, and about half as many.
- The default kernel of `:smooth` fits is `:b5`, so a fitted grid must be interpolated with
  `kernel = :b5` (uniform: `bc = :poly`) unless a kernel was given.
- `extrap = :natural` on nonuniform grids is an error; it was never the natural rule there.
- A `bc` other than the default on nonuniform grids is an error; it was ignored before.

##### Migration guide

- Code that interpolates a `:smooth` fit's grid with `kernel = :a4` (uniform) or `:n3`
  (nonuniform) should use `:b5`, or pass `kernel = :a4` / `:n3` to the fit to keep the old
  behaviour.
- Code that reads the knot count of an adaptive `:smooth` fit should take it from the
  returned axes.
- Remove `bc` from `convolution_interpolation` calls on nonuniform knots, and use
  `extrap = :line` or `:flat` where `:natural` was given on them.

## [v0.29.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.29.0) — 2026-10-20

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.29.0

[Diff since v0.28.2](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.28.2...v0.29.0)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.29.0

##### Adaptive and user-supplied grids in `fit_scattered`

`fit_scattered` can now place its knots where the points are. `grid = :adaptive` builds
nonuniform knot axes from the data's quantiles (blend `alpha`, adjacent-spacing cap `ratio`),
and `grid = (x_knots, y_knots, …)` uses axes you supply. Both modes work: `:exact` interpolates
clustered points that no uniform grid can separate, and `:smooth` reaches a given accuracy with
far fewer knots where the data vary. The nonuniform kernels are `:b5` (the `:exact` default)
and the cheap `:n3` (the `:smooth` default). The `:exact` warning and the `:smooth`
under-resolution warning now point to `grid = :adaptive` when it would help.

##### Better smoothing fits

`mode = :smooth` first fits on a grid as fine as the data, so that nothing the points resolve
is aliased into the residual, and then refits on the coarsest grid that resolves the smoothing
it found. Heavily smoothed signals now reach the smoothing GCV asks for on large data sets,
where the fine grid alone was too ill-conditioned to get there, and the returned grid is as
small as the fit allows. The `:exact` solver falls back to QR when Cholesky is not positive
definite, and the `:smooth` solver rejects a Cholesky solve whose residual says it is
inaccurate.

##### Numerics and infrastructure

- Nonuniform `:b` kernels extrapolate their ghost values in local coordinates, so a nonuniform
  interpolant is bit-identical under a translation of its grid.
- Tests run on Linux, macOS and Windows across the supported Julia versions; the adaptive-grid
  tests use deterministic low-discrepancy point sets.
- The package is archived on Zenodo and citeable from `CITATION.cff`.
- Documentation is moving from the README to [convinterp.org](https://convinterp.org), which
  covers this package and its Python port with executed examples and benchmarks against other
  packages. The README will shrink to a quick start in a coming release.

##### Breaking changes

- `fit_scattered(…; mode = :exact)` with `gridsize = :auto` now defaults `oversample` to 2.5
  in 2D and 2.0 in 3D and above (1.6 in 1D as before), so the grids it returns in two or more
  dimensions are finer than in v0.28.
- `fit_scattered(…; mode = :smooth)` returns a coarser grid than in v0.28 for smooth signals:
  the knot count is now set by the fitted smoothing, not by the data density alone.

##### Migration guide

- Code that reads the returned knot axes or coefficient array of a `fit_scattered` fit and
  assumes their size should take the size from the returned axes; the interpolant built from
  them is unchanged in use.
- To keep the v0.28 `:exact` grid density in 2D or 3D, pass `oversample = 1.6` explicitly.
- Nothing else changes: all existing calls run as before, and the new keywords `grid`,
  `alpha` and `ratio` are opt-in.

## [v0.28.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.28.0) — 2026-09-28

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.28.0

[Diff since v0.27.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.27.0...v0.28.0)

### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.28.0

#### Highlights

**Scattered data are now smoothed by default.** `fit_scattered` and `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` now use `mode = :smooth` unless told otherwise. Scattered data are usually measurements, and even a little noise is harmful under exact interpolation: the high-order kernels reproduce the noise and amplify it between the points, most of all in derivatives. With smoothing as the default, noisy data give sound results without any tuning, while noise-free data still come out close to interpolation. Trusted, noise-free data can opt into exact interpolation with `mode = :exact`.

**Faster, more reliable smoothing defaults.** `:smooth` now fits with the `:a4` kernel and roughness order `q = 5` for every kernel. With noisy data the accuracy is set by the noise rather than the kernel, and `:a4`'s narrow stencil makes the fit 2–3× faster than before in 2D and 3–9× faster in 3D, at comparable accuracy. Wider kernels such as `:b7` also become reliable in smoothing mode.

**Clearer feedback.** `:smooth` warns when the grid limit set by `oversample` stops the fit from resolving the chosen smoothing. It also raises a clear error when there are too few data points to smooth, which means 5^D or fewer: 25 in 2D, 125 in 3D.

#### Breaking changes

- The default `mode` of `fit_scattered` and of `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` is now `:smooth` instead of `:exact`. Calls without `mode` now smooth the data rather than interpolate it.
- With the new default, the third value returned by `fit_scattered` is the named tuple `(lambda, noise)` instead of the constraint violation `viol`.
- `:smooth` defaults to the `:a4` kernel and `q = 5`, so results of `mode = :smooth` without an explicit `kernel` or `q` differ slightly from v0.27.0.
- `:smooth` raises an error for 5^D or fewer data points.

#### Migration guide

- For exact interpolation of trusted data, add `mode = :exact`: `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` becomes `convolution_interpolation(points, values; mode = :exact)`, and the same applies to `fit_scattered`. Results are then identical to v0.27.0.
- Code that used the third return value of `fit_scattered` as `viol` should pass `mode = :exact`.
- For noisy data, no change is needed: the default now does the right thing. To reproduce v0.27.0's smoothing exactly, pass `kernel = :b5`.
- For very small data sets, use `mode = :exact`, or pass a lower `q`.

## [v0.27.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.27.0) — 2026-09-27

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.27.0

[Diff since v0.26.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.26.0...v0.27.0)

### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.27.0

#### Highlights

##### Smoothing of noisy scattered data: `mode = :smooth`

`fit_scattered` and `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` gain `mode = :smooth` for noisy scattered data. Instead of passing through every point, the fit balances closeness to the data against smoothness, and chooses that balance itself by generalized cross-validation, so there is no smoothing parameter to tune. The result is a high-order interpolant like any other: evaluate it, differentiate it, integrate it.

```julia
itp = convolution_interpolation(points, values; mode=:smooth)    # smoothing chosen automatically
knots, vals, info = fit_scattered(points, values; mode=:smooth)  # the fit, with diagnostics
info.noise                                                       # estimated noise level of the data
info.lambda                                                      # the chosen smoothing; pass it back to reproduce the fit
```

**Why it matters.** The previous options for noisy scattered data each needed hand-tuning and fell short. The `scattered_to_grid` + `convolution_smooth` pipeline left the imprint of the nearest-neighbour gridding in the result and blurred fine features. `mode = :lsq` fitted the noise at its default settings and only worked once its grid density was tuned by hand for each noise level and signal. In my comparisons, `:smooth` with its automatic choice matched or beat both of them even at their best hand-tuned settings, with lower errors in the values and derivatives. It also reports an estimate of the data's noise level, a useful check against a known measurement error. It stays fast: the fit's grid is refined only as far as the chosen smoothing needs.

#### Breaking changes

- `fit_scattered(...; mode = :lsq)` has been removed and now raises an `ArgumentError`. `mode = :smooth` replaces it.
- With `mode = :smooth`, the third value returned by `fit_scattered` is a named tuple `(lambda, noise)` instead of a number. `mode = :exact` still returns the constraint violation.

#### Deprecations

- `scattered_to_grid` is deprecated and will be removed in v1.0. It still works, with a one-time warning.

#### Migration guide

Least-squares fits of noisy scattered data:

```julia
# before
knots, vals, _ = fit_scattered(points, values; mode=:lsq, gridsize=14)
# after: the grid and the smoothing are chosen automatically
knots, vals, info = fit_scattered(points, values; mode=:smooth)
```

The gridding-and-smoothing pipeline:

```julia
# before
grid = scattered_to_grid(points, values, (xs, ys))
itp = convolution_interpolation((xs, ys), convolution_smooth((xs, ys), grid, 0.1))
# after: fit and smooth in one step
itp = convolution_interpolation(points, values; mode=:smooth)
```

The smoothed interpolant is defined on the data's bounding box rather than on a grid you choose, so evaluate inside that box, or pass `extrap`. For noisy data that is already on a grid, `convolution_smooth` remains the tool.

## [v0.26.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.26.0) — 2026-09-27

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.26.0

[Diff since v0.25.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.25.0...v0.26.0)

### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.26.0

#### Highlights

- **Lazy mode gives exactly eager's boundary values, in every dimension.** Lazy boundary cells now compute the same ghost points as eager construction, including the `:detect` boundary check. Lazy mode supports real boundary ghosts and derivatives in any dimension, and is thread-safe.
- **Lazy mode is chosen automatically for large grids.** With the new default `lazy=nothing`, a uniform grid is built lazily when eager expansion would be costly in memory (more than 2²⁷ coefficients) or construction time (more than 2²⁴ ghost points), and eagerly otherwise.
- **More accurate boundaries.** Ghost points are computed with compensated summation directly from the data, removing a rounding error that grew on N-D edges and corners.
- **Faster, simpler antiderivatives.** One evaluator handles every integral order, with exactly derived weights; first-order integrals in 2D and 3D evaluate up to 2× faster, and integral construction is much faster.

#### Bug fixes

- `convolution_interpolation(knots, values)` without keywords on nonuniform knots built a uniform interpolant; it now builds the nonuniform one, as the keyword call does.
- Grids with different knot types per axis (e.g. a range and a vector) failed on the nonuniform `b`-kernel path.
- Lazy interpolants mixing `:a0`/`:a1` axes with higher-order kernels failed at boundary cells.

#### Breaking changes

- `boundary_fallback` is deprecated and has no effect (a warning is shown; it will be removed in v1.0). Lazy interpolants that used `boundary_fallback=true` now return exact values near the boundaries instead of linear ones.
- The default for `lazy` is now `nothing` (chosen by grid size, see above) instead of `false`. Large grids are built lazily unless `lazy=false` is given; keyword-free calls in 4D are no longer lazy for small grids.
- Lazy interpolants with `bc=:detect` now follow eager's boundary decisions, so their values near the boundaries can differ from v0.25.
- Values near the boundaries and antiderivative values change at rounding level.
- First-order antiderivative interpolants display as `derivative=-1` instead of `integral`.

#### Migration guide

- Remove `boundary_fallback` from your calls.
- To keep eager construction regardless of grid size, pass `lazy=false`; to force lazy mode, pass `lazy=true`.
- Code that accessed internal fields of the interpolant types (such as `left_values`, the integral tail arrays, `lazy_workspace` or `boundary_fallback`) must be updated; these fields were removed.

## [v0.25.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.25.0) — 2026-09-24

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.25.0

[Diff since v0.24.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.24.0...v0.25.0)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.25.0

##### Highlights
- **Integrals of any order.** `derivative = -m` gives the m-fold antiderivative of the interpolant, anchored at zero at the leftmost interior knot, up to order 2 (`:a0`, `:a1`), 4 (other `:a` kernels), 6 (`:b5`) or 8 (`:b7`–`:b13`). All orders are computed from exactly derived kernel antiderivatives and converge at the kernel's full rate.
- **In any dimension, mixed freely.** Orders can be chosen per dimension and combined with interpolation or derivatives, e.g. `derivative = (-2, 0)` or `(-3, 1, -1)`.
- **Faster integrals.** Integral construction and evaluation do substantially less work, and mixed integral/derivative evaluation is 20–30% faster.

##### Fixes
- Lazy mode combined with an antiderivative now raises a clear error at construction, instead of failing at the first evaluation.

##### Breaking changes
- The internal fields and type parameters of `FastConvolutionInterpolation` for integrals have changed. This only affects code that accesses these internals directly.
- Mixed integral interpolants now display as `derivative=(…)` instead of `mixed=(…)`.

##### Migration guide
- No changes are needed for code using the public API.

This release was developed with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic).

## [v0.24.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.24.0) — 2026-09-24

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.24.0

[Diff since v0.23.2](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.23.2...v0.24.0)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.24.0

##### Highlights
- **Exact kernel evaluation.** The fast path no longer uses precomputed kernel tables. Kernel weights are computed exactly from each kernel's polynomial pieces, so values, derivatives and integrals are exact to rounding in any precision (`Float32`, `Float64`, `BigFloat`).
- **Faster evaluation**, especially in higher dimensions, e.g. 3D `:b13` from ~60 μs to under 1 μs per evaluation.
- **Nothing is written to disk.** The kernel table artifact and the on-disk cache are gone, and so are the Artifacts, Scratch and Serialization dependencies.

##### Fixes
- Pure N-D integrals (`derivative=-1` in all of 4 or more dimensions) skipped the trailing coefficients in every dimension and returned wrong values.
- On densely sampled grids, rounding in the grid spacing raised the error floor in proportion to the number of points. Values, derivatives, integrals and resampling now reach machine precision.

##### Deprecations
- The `precompute` and `subgrid` keywords no longer have any effect. They are still accepted, with a warning, and will be removed in a future release.

##### Breaking changes
- The type parameters of `FastConvolutionInterpolation` have changed. This only affects code that dispatches on or constructs that type with explicit parameters.
- Invalid `subgrid`/kernel combinations in `convolution_resample` no longer raise an error; the keyword is ignored with a deprecation warning.
- Results differ slightly from earlier versions, now being exact rather than table-interpolated.

##### Migration guide
- Remove `precompute` and `subgrid` from your calls.
- Optionally, delete the kernel cache written by earlier versions: `~/.julia/scratchspaces/75b5ba44-29d7-490a-960d-52c835d47405`.

## [v0.23.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/releases/tag/v0.23.0) — 2026-09-15

#### ConvolutionInterpolations v0.23.0

[Diff since v0.22.0](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl/compare/v0.22.0...v0.23.0)

#### ConvolutionInterpolations.jl v0.23.0

A release focused on error handling and kernel routing. No API changes; correct existing code behaves identically.

##### Breaking changes

- `FastConvolutionInterpolation` now throws on nonuniform grids. Previously a direct call with nonuniform knots was accepted and silently interpolated on the wrong spacing (the fast kernels are precomputed on a uniform subgrid and cannot adapt their weights). Code that relied on this path was producing incorrect results; see the migration guide below.

Nothing else changes behaviour for code that previously worked correctly. Two call forms that used to error now work (`:n3` on a uniform grid, and a direct `ConvolutionInterpolation` call with a `Symbol` kernel on a uniform grid).

##### Migration guide

If you construct `FastConvolutionInterpolation` directly and your knots are nonuniform in any dimension, switch to one of:

- `convolution_interpolation(knots, values; ...)` — the default entry point. It detects the grid and selects the fast path for uniform grids and the weight-adjusting slow path for nonuniform grids automatically. This is the recommended replacement.
- `ConvolutionInterpolation(knots, values; ...)` — the slow constructor, whose kernels adjust their weights to nonuniform spacing.

Calls through `convolution_interpolation` need no changes; it already routed nonuniform grids away from the fast path.

If you pass `:a4`, `:a5` or `:a7` on a nonuniform grid, nothing changes in behaviour — those calls errored before and still do — but the docstrings no longer claim a fallback to `:n3`. On nonuniform grids the supported kernels are `:a0`, `:a1`, `:a3`/`:n3` and the full `b`-series (`:b5`, `:b7`, `:b9`, `:b11`, `:b13`); all of these work on both uniform and nonuniform grids, with the `b`-series giving higher order at the cost of a per-interval weight projection on nonuniform data.

##### `:n3` and `:a3` are now interchangeable

The nonuniform cubic kernel `:n3` previously raised a `MethodError` on a fully uniform grid, because it has no uniform evaluator. It is now routed to `:a3`, which is mathematically identical on uniform grids and faster. #### Non-uniform path: much faster construction, rigorous convergence rates

The per-interval weight construction for non-uniform grids has been substantially optimized:

- **Extended-precision arithmetic replaces exact rationals** in the internal projection: BigFloat throughout, truncated to `Float64` only at the final storage step. Accuracy is unchanged; construction is dramatically faster.
- **Normalized local coordinates**: knot spacings are scaled per interval before the projection, making the system's conditioning independent of mesh size. Fine grids (tested to N = 10⁴ and beyond) now construct without numerical degradation.
- **QR factorization** for the projection solve, and **parallelized** per-interval computation (intervals are independent).

Together these make the non-uniform path viable at grid sizes where it was previously impractical.

The README now also states the **rigorous convergence rates** for non-uniform grids, verified in extended-precision arithmetic: the construction enforces polynomial reproduction up to each kernel's full degree, so convergence order is **degree + 1**: 6th order for `:b5`, 8th for `:b7`, 10th for `:b9`, 12th for `:b11`, and **14th order for `:b13`**. For `:b7` and above this *exceeds* the uniform design order of 7. On the classical Runge benchmark, `:b13` reaches Float64 machine precision at roughly 500 non-uniform samples.

#### Extended derivative support

Exact-arithmetic verification of the kernel piece polynomials showed the b-series kernels are **smoother than previously documented**: the family is C^(degree - 2), i.e. `:b7` is C⁵ (previously stated C⁴), `:b9` is C⁷, `:b11` is C⁹, and `:b13` is C¹¹. The `:b5` documentation was already exact (C³).

Following this, the fast-path derivative range has been extended by one order for `:b7` through `:b13`:

| Kernel | Continuity | Derivative range (was) |
|--------|-----------|------------------------|
| `:b7`  | C⁵  | 0..5 (0..4) |
| `:b9`  | C⁷  | 0..6 (0..5) |
| `:b11` | C⁹  | 0..7 (0..6) |
| `:b13` | C¹¹ | 0..7 (0..6) |

The line is drawn at the 7th derivative: although the kernels support deeper differentiation in exact arithmetic, derivative orders beyond 7 are dominated by roundoff noise amplification in Float64 (the chain-rule factor (1/h)ⁿ) and are deliberately not exposed on the fast path. The full ladder up to each kernel's continuity class remains reachable by evaluating the exact rational kernel coefficients directly in extended precision: undocumented and unsupported, but there for those who need it.

New derivative orders are convergent on non-uniform grids (order degree + 1 − n) and were validated against analytical derivatives on randomly perturbed grids.

None. The API is fully backwards compatible. One internal change may be observable: the non-uniform weight construction now uses extended-precision floating point instead of exact rational arithmetic, so stored `Float64` weights may differ from v0.20.x at the last-bit level. Convergence behavior is unchanged or improved.

#### Migration guide

No action required. Existing code runs unchanged; the new derivative orders and faster non-uniform construction are available immediately.

This release changes the default kernel selection to a dimension-dependent policy and fixes a long-standing boundary issue where evaluating at exact domain endpoints could throw under the default `extrap=:throw`.

#### Dimension-dependent default kernel

The default `kernel` keyword is now `:auto`, which selects the kernel based on dimension:

| Dimension | Default kernel |
|---|---|
| N ≤ 2 | `:b7` |
| N = 3 | `:b5` |
| N = 4–5 | `:a4` |
| N ≥ 6 | `:a3` |

The policy trades kernel width against tensor-product evaluation cost: in 1D and 2D the wider `:b7` kernel improves accuracy at near-negligible evaluation cost, while in higher dimensions the `(2·eqs)^N` support growth favors narrower kernels. The keyword constructors and the positional fast constructors now share a single policy and cannot drift apart.

Passing an explicit kernel symbol or tuple behaves exactly as before; `:auto` may also be passed explicitly to opt into the policy.

#### Boundary tolerance fix

Evaluating at exact domain endpoints — for example `itp(2π)` on knots `range(0, 2π, length=n)` — could previously throw a domain error under the default `extrap=:throw`, because the domain bounds are reconstructed from the expanded knot arithmetic and could differ from the original endpoints by one ulp.

Domain checks now allow ulp-scale slack (relative to the bound magnitudes, with an absolute floor near zero) and clamp near-boundary queries before evaluation. Exact endpoints and ulp-adjacent points evaluate correctly; genuinely out-of-domain points still throw. The tolerance forgives floating-point rounding, not user error.

#### Breaking changes

- **Default results change for constructions that did not specify a kernel.** A 1D or 2D construction with default arguments now uses `:b7` instead of `:b5`, producing slightly different (generally more accurate) values. Constructions with an explicit `kernel=` argument are unaffected.
- **Near-boundary behavior under `extrap=:throw` changes.** Queries within one ulp of the domain boundary previously threw and now evaluate. Code relying on the throw as a strict boundary detector at ulp precision will observe different behavior.

No exported function signatures were removed or renamed; the `kernel` keyword's default value changed from `:b5` to `:auto`.

#### Migration guide

- **To reproduce v0.19.x default results exactly:** pass `kernel=:b5` explicitly.
- **If you stored reference outputs** generated with default kernels in 1D or 2D, regenerate them or pin `kernel=:b5`.

##### Highlights

The headline feature of v0.14.0 is a new class of **fast mixed integral/derivative operators** that combine antiderivatives, derivatives, and interpolation across different dimensions in a single allocation-free evaluation call. This extends the fast antiderivative path introduced in v0.13.0, which accelerated pure antiderivatives using precomputed tail sums, to the fully general mixed case.

##### New Features

**Fast mixed integral/derivative operators**

In v0.13.0, `derivative=(-1,-1)` in 2D used tail sums to achieve O(stencil^2) evaluation independent of grid size for pure antiderivatives. v0.14.0 extends this to arbitrary mixtures of integrals, derivatives, and interpolation across dimensions. For example:
```julia
# integrate in x, differentiate in y, interpolate in z, single O(stencil^3) call
itp = convolution_interpolation((xs,ys,zs), vs; derivative=(-1, 1, 0))

# definite integral via differences cancels the unknown constant:
itp(x2, y, z) - itp(x1, y, z)  # ≈ ∫ₓ₁ˣ² f dx · ∂f/∂y · f(z)
```

The fast path uses precomputed tail sums to evaluate contributions from coefficients outside the local stencil in O(1) per integral dimension, reducing the total cost to O(stencil^N) where N is the number of dimensions, the same asymptotic cost as pure interpolation. This is achieved by decomposing the evaluation domain, each part handled by a dedicated lookup into precomputed tail sum arrays built at construction time.

Mixed operators are supported for any combination of integral (`-1`), interpolation (`0`), and derivative (`≥1`) orders per dimension, in any number of dimensions. Up to 3 integral dimensions use the specialized fast path; 4 or more integral dimensions fall back to a general accurate path.

The direct (non-fast) path for mixed operators is also available via `fast=false`, and agreement between fast and direct paths is verified in the test suite.

**End-to-end zero-allocation evaluation**

All non-lazy evaluation paths, including the extrapolation wrapper, are now verified allocation-free via `@allocated` tests. This covers all kernels (`:a0` through `:b13`), all derivative/integral/mixed combinations, and 1D through 4D. The key enabler was replacing runtime fields and symbol-based dispatch with compile-time singleton structs and `Val`-based type parameters throughout.

**BigFloat precision preservation**

All kernels correctly propagate `BigFloat` arithmetic through construction and evaluation without silent downcast to `Float64`. B-series kernels on dense grids (n=2000) achieve errors below `1e-16`, well below `Float64` precision, verified by new precision tests. This means the package can be used directly for extended precision computation by simply passing `BigFloat` grids and values.

**Expanded test suite**

Test count grows from 696 to 941, adding:
- Mixed integral/derivative convergence in 2D, 3D, 4D (fast and direct paths)

##### Breaking Change: `:detect` Kernel Boundary Condition Removed

The `:detect` kernel boundary condition has been removed. This option attempted to automatically
detect periodic signals and apply a mixed linear-prediction boundary condition per slice.
In practice, this per-slice detection was unreliable, different slices of the same 2D or 3D
array could receive different boundary conditions, creating asymmetric coefficient arrays and
degrading interpolation accuracy, particularly for wide kernels (`:b9`, `:b11`, `:b13`) with
few grid points.

**Migration guide:** Replace `kernel_bc=:detect` with one of:
- `kernel_bc=:polynomial`, optimal for most cases, preserves polynomial reproduction (default when sufficient points)
- `kernel_bc=:auto`, uses `:polynomial` when sufficient points, falls back to `:linear` automatically
- `kernel_bc=:linear`, safe, stable fallback for any function type
- `kernel_bc=:quadratic`, second-order extrapolation (use with caution on wide kernels)
- `kernel_bc=:periodic`, for known periodic signals with insufficient points for `:polynomial`

The default fallback for insufficient grid points has also changed from `:detect` to `:linear`.
The `:linear` kernel boundary condition is unconditionally stable, it never produces the unbounded ghost point
growth that the `:quadratic` kernel boundary condition can exhibit on small grids with wide kernels.

---

##### Fast Antiderivative: O(eqs) in 1D, O(eqs^2) in 2D

The fast path for `derivative=-1` has been fundamentally redesigned. Previously, despite being
called "fast", the antiderivative evaluation looped over the entire coefficient array, O(N)
per eval in 1D, O(N^2) in 2D, giving no advantage over the direct path for large grids.

**What changed:** The kernel antiderivative K̃(s) saturates to exactly +/- ½ outside the stencil
support. This means the contribution of all coefficients outside the local stencil can be
precomputed at construction time as a cumulative sum, the "tail". At evaluation, the total
integral decomposes into:

- **Local stencil** (O(eqs) terms): per-j kernel lookup, unchanged from before
- **Left/right tails** (O(1)): precomputed prefix sums, single array lookup

In 2D, the domain decomposes into 9 quadrants around the stencil. The four corner quadrants
(both dimensions in tail) are O(1) via 2D cross-sum arrays. The four edge quadrants (one
dimension in stencil, one in tail) are O(eqs) via 1D prefix lookups. Only the center quadrant
(both in stencil) requires the O(eqs^2) double loop.

**Speedup at N=200:**

| Kernel | Fast vs direct |
|--------|---------------|
| `:a3`  | 115x          |
| `:b5`  | 44x           |
| `:b7`  | 1,513x        |
| `:b11` | 1,957x        |
| `:b13` | 2,117x        |

At N=1000, speedups reach **11,000x** for `:b13`. Evaluation time is now flat (O(1) in N)
for all grid sizes.

---

**Polynomial path (right boundary sign fix):** The polynomial kernel boundary condition (`:polynomial`) matrix is
applied to the reversed signal at right boundaries. A curvature continuity check now correctly
determines whether the ghost points need to be negated, handling even functions (cosine-like)
and odd functions (sine-like) correctly in all dimensions. Previously, a hardcoded dimension
check (`dim == 1`) was used, which failed for even functions in the second dimension.

boundaries, consistent with the polynomial path. This fixes asymmetric coefficient arrays

New `lazy` keyword argument for all constructors. When `lazy=true`, ghost point expansion is skipped at construction time — boundary ghost values are computed on the fly during evaluation only when the stencil reaches near a domain boundary. Interior evaluation is identical to eager mode.

New `boundary_fallback` keyword argument. #### How it works

On uniform grids, kernel weights are the same for every interval. On non-uniform grids, each interval needs its own weights adapted to the local grid geometry. This is achieved by expanding the kernel in a binomial series (using Rational{BigInt} arithmetic to avoid floating-point contamination in the weight generation) around each interval's local coordinate, then projecting through a Vandermonde system to enforce polynomial reproduction up to the kernel's design order. The result is a compact set of polynomial coefficients per interval, evaluated via Horner's method at query time.

Ghost point values near domain boundaries are also computed via Vandermonde solves using Rational{BigInt} arithmetic.

- Non-uniform b-kernels: `:b5` through `:b13` now work on non-uniform grids with per-interval weight polynomials precomputed via exact Rational{BigInt} arithmetic

- `:n3` kernel: Dedicated non-uniform cubic kernel equivalent to non-uniform Catmull-Rom splines. All `:a` kernels fall back to `:n3` on non-uniform grids
- Zero-allocation evaluation: ~40ns per point via Horner's method

#### 🔧 Migration Guide

##### Minimal Migration (Keep Existing Behavior)
If you want to maintain exact previous behavior:
```julia
# Change from:
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y)

# To:
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; degree=:a3, kernel_bc=:detect, precompute=1_000)
```

##### Recommended Migration (Adopt New Defaults)
Most users should simply update their code to use the new defaults, which provide better accuracy and performance:
```julia
# Old code
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y)  # Was :a3

# New code - no changes needed, now uses :b5!
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y)
```

The b5 kernel with polynomial boundary conditions provides superior accuracy (7th order vs 4th order) with comparable performance to the old cubic default.

##### Memory-Constrained Environments
If memory is extremely limited (embedded systems, etc.):
```julia
# Reduce precompute resolution (degrades accuracy slightly)
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; precompute=10_000)

# Or disable fast mode entirely (slower but minimal memory)
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; fast=false)
```

##### High-Precision Applications
For applications requiring extended precision:
```julia
# Use BigFloat with desired precision
setprecision(512)  # 512-bit precision
x = big.(your_data_x)
y = big.(your_data_y)
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y)  # Automatically uses BigFloat
```

#### 🔬 Technical Details

##### Kernel Discovery Method
The b-series kernels were discovered through systematic analytical search using SymPy:
1. Formulate boundary value problem as symbolic equations
2. Exhaustively search boundary condition combinations
3. Verify polynomial reproduction via Taylor series expansion
4. Validate frequency domain characteristics via FFT analysis
5. Select kernels with optimal accuracy/smoothness balance

This automated discovery process generalizes the approach of Keys (1981) to arbitrary polynomial degrees, enabling kernels that would be intractable to derive by hand.

##### Exact Rational Storage
Kernel coefficients stored as `Rational{Int}`:
```julia
# Example b5 kernel coefficient
-1228311859//656862720  # Exact rational, not Float64
```

This enables:
- Arbitrary precision evaluation
- No accumulated rounding errors in coefficient storage
- Reproducible results across platforms and precision levels
